source_text: Ἀνάγκη δὲ ἀπολογούμενον ἀκριβεστέρους παρέχειν τοὺς λογισμοὺς καὶ περὶ τῶν ὀνομάτων, ὅτι νεώτερα, καὶ περὶ τῶν εἰκόνων, ὅτι χθὲς καὶ πρώην γεγόνασιν, ὡς λόγῳ εἰπεῖν· ἴστε δὲ καὶ ὑμεῖς ταῦτα ἀξιολογώτερον, ὡς ἂν ἐν πᾶσι καὶ ὑπὲρ πάντας τοῖς παλαιοῖς συγγινόμενοι. Φημὶ οὖν Ὀρφέα καὶ Ὅμηρον καὶ Ἡσίοδον εἶναι τοὺς καὶ γένη καὶ ὀνόματα δόντας τοῖς ὑπ᾿ αὐτῶν λεγομένοις θεοῖς. Μαρτυρεῖ δὲ καὶ Ἡρόδοτος· Ἡσίοδον γὰρ καὶ Ὅμηρον ἡλικίην τετρακοσίοις ἔτεσι δοκέω πρεσβυτέρους ἐμοῦ γενέσθαι, καὶ οὐ πλείοσι· οὗτοι δέ εἰσιν οἱ ποιήσαντες θεογονίην Ἕλλησι, καὶ τοῖσι θεοῖσι τὰς ἐπωνυμίας δόντες καὶ τιμάς τε καὶ τέχνας διελόντες, καὶ εἴδεα αὐτῶν σημήναντες. Αἱ δ᾿ εἰκόνες, μέχρι μήπω πλαστικὴ καὶ γραφικὴ καὶ ἀνδριαντοποιητικὴ ἦσαν, οὐδὲ ἐνομίζοντο, Σαυρίου δὲ τοῦ Σαμίου καὶ Κράτωνος τοῦ Σικυωνίου καὶ Κλεάνθους τοῦ Κορινθίου καὶ κόρης Κορινθίας ἐπιγενομένων· καὶ σκιαγραφίας μὲν εὑρεθείσης ὑπὸ Σαυρίου, ἵππον ἐν ἡλίῳ περιγράψαντος, γραφικῆς δὲ ὑπὸ Κράτωνος, ἐν πίνακι λελευκωμένῳ σκιὰς ἀνδρὸς καὶ γυναικὸς ἐναλείψαντος· ἀπὸ δὲ τῆς κόρης ἡ κοροπλαθικὴ εὑρέθη· ἐρωτικῶς γάρ τινος ἔχουσα περιέγραψεν αὐτοῦ κοιμωμένου ἐν τοίχῳ τὴν σκιάν, εἶθ᾿ ὁ πατήρ, ἡσθεὶς ἀπαραλλάκτῳ οὔσῃ τῇ ὁμοιότητι, (κέραμον δὲ εἰργάζετο) ἀναγλύψας τὴν περιγραφὴν πηλῷ προσανεπλήρωσεν· ὁ τύπος ἔτι καὶ νῦν ἐν Κορίνθῳ σώζεται. Τούτοις δὲ ἐπιγενόμενοι Δαίδαλος καὶ Θεόδωρος ὁ Μιλήσιος ἀνδριαντοποιητικὴν καὶ πλαστικὴν προσεξεῦρον. Ὁ μὲν δὴ χρόνος ὀλίγος τοσοῦτος ταῖς εἰκόσι καὶ τῇ περὶ τὰ εἴδωλα πραγματείᾳ, ὡς ἔχειν εἰπεῖν τὸν ἑκάστου τεχνίτην θεοῦ. Τὸ μὲν γὰρ ἐν Ἐφέσῳ τῆς Ἀρτέμιδος καὶ τὸ τῆς Ἀθηνᾶς (μᾶλλον δὲ Ἀθηλᾶς· Ἀθηλᾶ γὰρ ὡς οἱ μυστικώτερον, οὕτω γὰρ τὸ ἀπὸ τῆς ἐλαίας τὸ παλαιὸν) καὶ τὴν καθημένην Ἔνδοιος εἰργάσατο μαθητὴς Δαιδάλου, ὁ δὲ Πύθιος ἔργον Θεοδώρου καὶ Τηλεκλέους, καὶ ὁ Δήλιος καὶ ἡ Ἄρτεμις Τεκταίου καὶ Ἀγγελίωνος τέχνη, ἡ δὲ ἐν Σάμῳ Ἥρα καὶ ἐν Ἄργει Σμίλιδος χεῖρες, καὶ Φειδίου τὰ λοιπὰ εἴδωλα, ἡ Ἀφροδίτη ἐν Κνίδῳ ἑταίρα Πραξιτέλους τέχνη, ὁ ἐν Ἐπιδαύρῳ Ἀσκληπιὸς ἔργον Φειδίου. Συνελόντα φάναι, οὐδὲν αὐτῶν διαπέφευγεν τὸ μὴ ὑπ᾿ ἀνθρώπου γεγονέναι. Εἰ τοίνυν θεοί, τί οὐκ ἦσαν ἐξ ἀρχῆς; Τί δαί εἰσι νεώτεροι τῶν πεποιηκότων; Τί δαὶ ἔδει αὐτοῖς πρὸς τὸ γενέσθαι ἀνθρώπων καὶ τέχνης; Γῆ ταῦτα καὶ λίθοι καὶ ὕλη καὶ περίεργος τέχνη.
thought_title: Recent Origin of Gods' Names and Images
pass_a_gloss: It is necessary for one making a defense to provide more precise thoughts also about the names, that they are recent, and about the images, that they came into being yesterday and the day before, so to speak; and you know these things are more worthy of consideration, as being in agreement with all the ancients and beyond all the ancients. I say then that Orpheus and Homer and Hesiod are the ones who gave both the families and the names to the gods spoken of under them. And Herodotus bears witness; for I think Hesiod and Homer are older than me by about four hundred years, and not much more; these are the ones who made the theogony for the Greeks, and gave the epithets to the gods and divided the honors and arts among them, and indicated their forms. The images, until the plastic and graphic and statue-making arts were not yet in existence, were not considered to exist, until the time of Saurius the Samian and Craton the Sicyonian and Cleanthus the Corinthian and a Corinthian maiden; and the art of shading was discovered by Saurius, who drew a horse in the sun, and the graphic art by Craton, who smeared the shadows of a man and a woman on a whitened board; and from the maiden the art of coroplasty was discovered; for having an erotic passion for someone, she drew his shadow while he was sleeping on a wall, and then her father, delighted by the exact likeness, (he worked with clay) carved out the drawing and filled it in with clay; and the model is still preserved in Corinth. And following these, Daedalus and Theodorus the Milesian further developed the statue-making and plastic arts. The time is so short for the images and the business of idols, that it is possible to say that each craftsman is the god. For the one in Ephesus of Artemis and the one of Athena (or rather Athela; for Athela is, as the mystics say, the ancient name derived from the olive) and the seated Endoios were made by a student of Daedalus, and the Pythian is a work of Theodorus and Telecleus, and the Delian and the Artemis are the work of Tectaeus and Angelion, and the Hera in Samos and the Smilis in Argos are the work of hands, and the rest of the idols are the work of Phidias, and the Aphrodite in Cnidus is the work of Praxiteles, and the Asclepius in Epidaurus is a work of Phidias. To sum up, none of these has escaped being made by a human. If then they are gods, why did they not exist from the beginning? Why are they younger than their makers? Why did they need humans and art to come into being? Earth, stones, wood, and elaborate art are what they are made of.
pass_b_english: A defense requires precise reasoning about the names of the gods, since they are recent, and about their images, since they appeared only yesterday and the day before, so to speak. You know these facts are especially worthy of attention, because they harmonize with all ancient testimony and surpass it. I assert that Orpheus, Homer, and Hesiod are the very ones who supplied both the genealogies and the names to the gods spoken of under them. Herodotus bears witness: he judges Hesiod and Homer to be about four hundred years older than himself, and not much more; these are the poets who composed the Greek theogony, assigned the gods their epithets, distributed their honors and arts, and described their forms. As for images, they were not even thought to exist until the arts of modeling, drawing, and statue-making arose — until the time of Saurius of Samos, Craton of Sicyon, Cleanthus of Corinth, and a Corinthian maiden. Saurius invented skiagraphy by tracing a horse in sunlight; Craton invented graphic art by sketching the shadows of a man and a woman on a whitened panel; and the maiden invented coroplasty when, driven by erotic longing, she traced her lover’s shadow on a wall while he slept. Her father, a potter, delighted in the exact likeness, carved out the outline, and filled it with clay; the model is still preserved in Corinth. After them, Daedalus and Theodorus of Miletus advanced statue-making and modeling. The timespan for images and the whole business of idols is so short that one can say each craftsman is the god he fashions. The Artemis at Ephesus, the Athena — or rather Athela, since the mystics call her Athela, the ancient name derived from the olive — and the seated statue by Endoios, a pupil of Daedalus; the Pythian Apollo, a work of Theodorus and Telecleus; the Delian Apollo and Artemis, the work of Tectaeus and Angelion; the Hera in Samos and the Smilis in Argos, made by human hands; the remaining idols, the work of Phidias; the Aphrodite at Cnidus, the work of Praxiteles; the Asclepius at Epidaurus, a work of Phidias. In short, not one of them has escaped being made by a human. If they are gods, why did they not exist from the beginning? Why are they younger than their makers? Why did they need human beings and art to come into being? They are earth, stone, wood, and elaborate craftsmanship — nothing more.

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the nuances of the Greek text, including the parenthetical note on the clay work and the specific distinction between Athena and Athela. Pass A and Pass B are consistent with the Greek source.

Pass A: 'I say then that Orpheus and Homer and Hesiod are the ones who gave both the families and the names to the gods spoken of under them.' Pass B: 'I assert that Orpheus, Homer, and Hesiod are the very ones who supplied both the genealogies and the names to the gods spoken of under them.'
